common_name: Apricot Twist Wallflower (Long-Blooming Peachy-Orange Perennial Wallflower)

planting.note: Set out container-grown plants in spring into lean, well-drained soil in full sun; this cultivar is propagated by cuttings rather than seed.

directions: Plant rooted cuttings or container specimens in spring in average to lean, sharply drained soil in full sun; 'Apricot Twist' forms a tidy, bushy mound of gray-green foliage topped with dense spikes of warm orange-apricot flowers that soften to a peachy blush as they age, giving a two-tone color effect within the same flower cluster. Bloom begins in early spring and, if deadheaded, continues in flushes well into summer, making it a valuable long-season companion to silver-leaved Mediterranean plants like santolina and lavender. Avoid heavy or poorly drained soil, which shortens its lifespan; refresh plants from cuttings every few years as the woody crown ages.

common_name: Winter Orchid Wallflower (Coppery-to-Purple Mounding Perennial Wallflower)

planting.note: Set out container-grown plants in spring or fall into lean, well-drained soil in full sun to light afternoon shade; part of the Winter series bred for an extended cool-season bloom period.

directions: Plant container-grown specimens in average, sharply drained soil in full sun; 'Winter Orchid' opens with rust-red-to-coppery-orange buds that mature to a rich orchid-purple, creating a multicolored effect across each flower spike as older and newer blooms overlap. It forms a dense, rounded mound of narrow gray-green leaves and flowers from early spring through summer, rebounding after a light shearing and deadheading. Like other perennial wallflowers, it fades quickly in wet or heavy soil, so lean, well-drained sites are essential for a long-lived planting.
sources: North Carolina State Extension — Plants Database

common_name: Poem Lilac Wallflower (Fragrant Lilac-Purple Compact Perennial Wallflower)

planting.note: Set out container-grown plants in spring into lean, well-drained, slightly alkaline soil in a full-sun, sheltered site; part of the Poem series of hybrid wallflowers bred for extended, nonstop bloom.

directions: Plant container-grown specimens in average to lean, sharply drained soil in a sunny, sheltered spot; 'Poem Lilac' forms a small, shrubby mound of gray-green, sword-shaped leaves topped by deep burgundy buds that open into a profusion of sweetly scented, lilac-purple flowers from early spring through fall in mild climates. It is one of the more compact of the perennial hybrid wallflowers, making it well suited to border edges, rockeries, and mixed containers. Shear lightly after each bloom flush to keep growth dense and encourage the next round of flowers; excellent drainage prevents the crown rot that shortens the life of many wallflower hybrids.
sources: North Carolina State Extension — Plants Database

common_name: Chelsea Jacket Wallflower (Color-Changing Yellow-to-Purple Perennial Wallflower)

planting.note: Set out container-grown plants in spring into lean, well-drained soil in full sun; this RHS Award of Garden Merit cultivar is propagated by cuttings and does not come true from seed.

directions: Plant rooted cuttings or container specimens in average, sharply drained soil in full sun; 'Chelsea Jacket' is a low, spreading, short-lived perennial wallflower whose flowers open bright yellow and shift through tangerine to deep purple as they age, so a single flower spike often displays several colors at once. Its compact, somewhat prostrate habit suits the front of a border, dry stone walls, or a container where the color-changing display can be appreciated up close. Deadhead and shear lightly after the main spring-to-summer flush to prolong bloom, and take cuttings periodically since plants tend to decline after a few years, especially in heavy or wet soils.
sources: Great Plant Picks (Elisabeth C. Miller Botanical Garden)

common_name: Rosenrot Red Valerian (Uniform Rose-Pink Jupiter's Beard)

planting.note: Set out container-grown plants in spring into lean, well-drained, alkaline soil in full sun; this German-raised selection is a named color form of red valerian.

directions: Plant container specimens in spring in poor to average, well-drained, slightly alkaline soil in full sun; 'Rosenrot' bears dense, rounded clusters of clear rose-pink flowers that are more uniform and saturated in color than the variable pink-to-red tones of the wild species. It blooms from early summer into early autumn and thrives in the same lean, dry, rocky conditions favored by the species, becoming floppy and short-lived if grown in rich or wet soil. Shear plants back hard after the first flowering flush to encourage a tidy rebloom and to curb self-seeding, which can revert toward the straight species' color range if other Centranthus forms are nearby.

common_name: Lemon Queen Cotton Lavender (Pale Creamy-Yellow Gray Santolina)

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or container plants in spring in very well-drained, lean, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; grows a little taller than the species type.

directions: Plant rooted cuttings or container plants in spring in very well-drained, lean, slightly alkaline soil in full sun; 'Lemon Queen' shares the finely dissected, woolly, silver-gray foliage of gray santolina but bears pale, creamy-lemon-yellow button flowers rather than the species' bright gold, giving it a softer look in pastel and silver-themed plantings. It requires the same superb drainage as the species and will rot in wet, heavy, or humid conditions without excellent airflow. Shear after flowering to keep growth compact and prevent the woody, gappy center that develops on unpruned plants.

common_name: Edward Bowles Santolina (Pale Primrose-Yellow Rosemary-Leaved Lavender Cotton)

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings in spring in very well-drained, lean, poor soil in a sunny, sheltered site; reaches full size over several years.

directions: Plant rooted cuttings in spring in very well-drained, lean, sandy or gritty soil in a sunny, sheltered position; 'Edward Bowles' carries long, finely cut, rosemary-like gray-green leaves that are more feathery and open in texture than gray santolina's coral-like foliage, and it produces masses of pale, primrose-yellow button flowers in summer. Its taller, looser habit makes it a good textural foil for both silver and green Mediterranean subshrubs in a gravel garden or mixed dry border. Shear hard after flowering to maintain a rounded shape, since unpruned plants become open and leggy at the base within a few seasons.

common_name: Primrose Gem Green Santolina (Compact Pale-Yellow Lavender Cotton)

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings in spring in very well-drained, lean, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; a compact, RHS Award of Garden Merit selection of green santolina.

directions: Plant rooted cuttings in spring in very well-drained, lean, slightly alkaline soil in full sun; 'Primrose Gem' forms a neat, rounded mound of bright emerald-green, feathery foliage studded in midsummer with soft primrose-yellow button flowers, staying noticeably more compact than the straight green santolina species. Its tidy size makes it well suited to low edging, gravel gardens, and rockeries where a larger santolina would overwhelm the scale. Shear lightly after flowering to keep the mound dense and prevent the bare, woody centers that develop on neglected plants.

planting.note: Set out rooted cuttings or nursery starts after all danger of frost; grown as a fast-filling annual trailer outside zone 9-11 and as a woody perennial subshrub within it.

directions: Set out rooted cuttings or nursery starts after the last frost in average, well-drained soil in full sun; Helichrysum petiolare is a South African subshrub grown for its densely felted, round, silver-gray leaves that release a mild licorice-like scent when brushed, rather than for its small, insignificant white flowers, which are best pinched off to keep foliage full. Its vigorous, trailing stems make it a classic 'spiller' for mixed containers and hanging baskets, cascading a foot or more over the rim in a single season. Established plants tolerate drought well but benefit from regular watering in containers; where hardy, it forms a sprawling evergreen mound that can be cut back hard in spring to renew dense growth.

planting.note: Set out rooted cuttings or nursery starts after all danger of frost; an RHS Award of Garden Merit chartreuse-leaved sport of the species.

directions: Set out rooted cuttings or nursery starts after the last frost in average, well-drained soil in full sun to light afternoon shade in hot climates; 'Limelight' carries the same soft, velvety, rounded leaves as the species but in a glowing chartreuse-to-lime-green that releases a warm licorice scent in hot weather. Its trailing stems make it a favored 'hot color' spiller for mixed containers, playing off purple and burgundy foliage companions. In regions with intense summer sun, a little afternoon shade helps prevent the pale foliage from scorching or bleaching; pinch stem tips periodically to keep growth dense rather than leggy.

common_name: Variegated Licorice Plant (Cream-and-Gray Marbled Trailing Foliage)

planting.note: Set out rooted cuttings or nursery starts after all danger of frost; slower and less vigorous than the plain green species.

directions: Set out rooted cuttings or nursery starts after the last frost in average, well-drained soil in partial sun to bright, open shade; 'Variegatum' has felted, gray-green leaves irregularly marked with cream, the variegation often showing more strongly in cooler weather and settling to a softer silvery cream in summer heat. It is noticeably less vigorous and more compact than the plain green species, making it useful for scaled-down containers, window boxes, and shaded entry pots where its pale foliage brightens a dim corner. Pinch tips occasionally to encourage branching, and remove any all-green reverted shoots promptly, since they grow faster and can overtake the variegated portions of the plant.
sources: North Carolina State Extension — Plants Database
